newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Chrysler signs deal to make trucks in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chrysler signs deal to make trucks in Brazil.

text.p: U.S. carmaker Chrysler Corp signed a deal to build a $315 million Dakota pick-up truck plant in southern Brazil on Thursday, strengthening its presence in South America's booming Mercosur customs union.

Chrysler will break ground this year on the new plant, which will produce 12,000 units a year by 1998 and create 400 direct jobs in the southern state of Parana. Production is expected to begin at the end of the second quarter of 1998.
"We plan to begin operations with 400 employees and hit 1,000 when we reach annual capacity of 40,000 units," said Chrysler Corp president and chairman Robert J. Eaton.
Next month, Chrysler will open its first production facility in the four-nation Mercosur customs union in Cordoba, Argentina. It also has a plant in Venezuela.

Earlier today, Eaton and Parana state Governor Jaime Lerner formalized an agreement to build the plant, which will be Chrysler's first Dakota unit outside the U.S. and the company's third facility in South America.
Eaton said he chose Parana because of its transportation and telecommunications facilities, its market access, its proximity to suppliers and other Mercosur countries, and the quality of life.

Parana state also upped the stakes by offering tax incentives, in particular a deferral in paying the so-called ICMS tax. But Eaton said the incentive was a secondary factor in the company's decision to build the plant in the state.
"We will be here forever and the incentives are only for a short-term period," he said.
Eaton also said Brazil was chosen because of its strong growth prospects.
"There is no question that right now the biggest market is Brazil," he said.

Chrysler plans to build gasoline and diesel-powered Dakota pick-up trucks in a plant in Compa Largo, 18 miles (30 km) from Curitiba. The firm plans to sell 60 percent of its output in Brazil, with the remainder going to other Mercosur nations and the rest of Latin America.
Eaton also said the company has no intention of competing in Brazil's passenger car market. It wants to continue in its core products: pick-up trucks, mini-vans and sport utility vehicles.
"We don't expect to be a major player in the popular segment in Latin America. We have our own strategy," he said.

Within 60 days, the company is also expected to announce the location of a $500 million motor plant it will build with Germany's Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG (BMW). Eaton said he favors Brazil, although he noted Argentina is also being considered.
"It is most likely to be Brazil," he said.

When Chrysler completes its plant with BMW, the company will have invested nearly $1.0 billion in Latin America. Chrysler is investing $165 million in a sport utility plant in Cordoba, Argentina, which is expected to start production next month.
It also has invested between $80 million and $100 million in Venezuela.

Latin American operations, excluding Mexico, represent a small fraction of Chrysler's activities. Last year, only one percent of the company's $62 billion in global revenue came from Latin America. Eaton said, however, he expects that to grow to three percent by 2001.
